speakers_covered: Goldman Sachs (David Mericle / Jan Hatzius, GS Research)
BofA Global Research (Aditya Bhave, Stephen Juneau)

items.speaker: J.P. Morgan economists (note; authors not named on page)
items.occasion: Research note dated Friday Jan 9 after December jobs report, reported by Reuters Jan 12
items.quote: If the labor market weakens again in the coming months, or if inflation falls materially, the Fed could still ease later this year,
items.summary: J.P. Morgan withdrew its call for a January cut and now forecasts the next Fed move to be a 25bp hike in Q3 2027. It allows that easing later in 2026 is still possible if labor weakens or inflation falls materially, but expects the labor market to tighten by Q2 and disinflation to be gradual.
items.score_note: Base case removes all 2026 cuts and makes the next move a hike (2027); hike is distant, so +1 not +2.
items.call: no cuts in 2026; next move a 25bp hike in Q3 2027 (January cut call withdrawn)

items.speaker: Goldman Sachs economists (note; authors not named on page)
items.occasion: Research note dated Sunday Jan 11, reported by Reuters Jan 12
items.quote: If the labor market stabilizes as we expect, the FOMC will likely shift from risk management mode to normalization mode,
items.summary: Goldman pushed its two 2026 cuts back to June and September from March and June after the December jobs report, and lowered its 12-month US recession probability to 20% from 30%.
items.score_note: Still forecasts two cuts in 2026 but later; cuts not imminent, so -1.
items.call: 2026: two cuts, June and September (previously March and June)

items.speaker: Rick Rieder
items.role: Head of global fixed income, BlackRock (as described on page)
items.occasion: CNBC interview on Jan 12, quoted by Fortune (Jan 28)
items.quote: The Fed’s got to get the rate down to 3%
items.summary: Rieder, then a finalist for Fed chair, said the Fed has to get the policy rate down to 3% from 3.50-3.75%.
items.score_note: Explicitly says the Fed must cut by another 50bp or more; a should statement, not a forecast.
items.call: Fed should cut the funds rate to 3%

items.speaker: BofA Global Research (note; authors not named on page)
items.occasion: Research note after December jobs report, quoted in Reuters Jan 12
items.quote: Mix of data is consistent with our view that breakeven job growth might be falling (labor supply shock) even faster than the Fed will concede,
items.summary: BofA kept its forecast of cuts in June and July 2026 after the December jobs report, arguing breakeven job growth is falling because of a labor supply shock.
items.score_note: Maintains two cuts in mid-2026; not imminent.
items.call: 2026: two cuts, June and July (maintained)

items.speaker: Wells Fargo Research Team (Wells Fargo Economics)
items.occasion: Wells Fargo US Economic Outlook: January 2026, syndicated in full on FXStreet under the Wells Fargo Research Team byline
items.quote: We are sticking with our previous forecast of two 25 bps rate cuts in March and June, followed by a long pause at 3.00%-3.25% for the federal funds rate.
items.summary: Wells Fargo Economics kept its call for cuts in March and June, citing a labor market modestly on the wrong side of full employment and encouraging core inflation, but said the window for more cuts is closing and risks are skewed toward later and/or less easing.
items.score_note: Earliest cut call among the houses (March), but two meetings away and with risks flagged toward less easing; between -2 and -1, chose -1.
items.call: 2026: two cuts, March and June, then a long pause at 3.00%-3.25%

items.speaker: Goldman Sachs Research (firm article citing David Mericle, chief US economist)
items.occasion: Goldman Sachs Insights article on the 2026 US outlook, dated Jan 15, 2026
items.quote: Goldman Sachs Research predicts that the Fed will deliver rate cuts of 25 basis points each in June and September
items.summary: Goldman Sachs Research forecast above-consensus growth and below-consensus inflation for 2026 and two 25bp cuts in June and September, ending the cycle at 3%-3.25%.
items.score_note: Two cuts in 2026, mid-year onward; firm-authored article text rather than a quotation of an individual.
items.call: 2026: two cuts, June and September, to a terminal 3%-3.25%

items.speaker: Michael Feroli
items.occasion: J.P. Morgan Global Research web article on the Fed's next move (version dated January 16, 2026; archived Jan 22)
items.quote: The recent stabilization in the unemployment rate should finally bring some cohesion to the FOMC, and we now look for the Committee to be on hold at the January meeting.
items.summary: J.P. Morgan Global Research no longer sees a January cut, expects the Fed on hold through 2026 at 3.5-3.75%, and projects a 25bp hike in Q3 2027. Feroli added that easing later this year is possible if labor weakens or inflation falls materially.
items.score_note: Public restatement of the Jan 9 call: no 2026 cuts and next move a hike in 2027; hike is distant, so +1.
items.call: on hold through 2026; 25bp hike in Q3 2027

items.speaker: Jeremy Schwartz
items.occasion: Reuters poll of economists (Jan 16-21)
items.quote: we suspect the new leadership will likely manage to get another 50 basis points of rate cuts later in the year
items.summary: Schwartz said the economic outlook on its face argues for a hold and maybe even putting hikes on the table later, but Nomura expects the Fed on hold through the rest of Powell's term (May) and then 50bp of cuts later in 2026 under the new chair.
items.score_note: Base case is 50bp of cuts later in 2026, driven by new leadership rather than data; mentions hikes as what the data alone might suggest.
items.call: on hold through Powell's term (May); 50bp of cuts later in 2026 under new Fed leadership

items.speaker: Michael Gapen
items.occasion: Morgan Stanley Thoughts on the Market podcast, quarterly economics roundtable (recorded Thursday Jan 22, 10am New York)
items.quote: If that's the case, then we think the Fed can execute one or two more rate cuts.
items.summary: Gapen said tariff pass-through should last through Q1, after which inflation pressures diminish and the Fed can deliver one or two more cuts, which Morgan Stanley has in the second half of the year.
items.score_note: Expects one or two more cuts in 2026, conditional on inflation easing.
items.call: 2026: one or two more cuts, in the second half of the year, if inflation comes down

items.speaker: Goldman Sachs economists (FOMC preview; authors not named on page)
items.occasion: Goldman Sachs preview of the January 27-28 FOMC, quoted by investingLive
items.quote: We have penciled in the next 25bp rate cut in June, followed by a final cut in September to 3-3.25%.
items.summary: Ahead of the January meeting Goldman expected an uneventful hold, saying the FOMC had just delivered three cuts and is well positioned while it assesses their impact; it kept its path of a June cut and a final September cut to 3-3.25%.
items.score_note: Two more cuts in 2026 but not before June.
items.call: 2026: two cuts, June and September, to a terminal 3-3.25%

items.speaker: Morgan Stanley economists (FOMC preview; authors not named on page)
items.occasion: Morgan Stanley preview of the January 27-28 FOMC, quoted by investingLive
items.quote: We expect the Fed to remain on hold at its January meeting, keeping the target range for the federal funds rate at 3.5-3.75%.
items.summary: Morgan Stanley expected a January hold with the easing-bias language retained, and expected Powell to deliver a dovish hold that still points to further rate cuts rather than a durable pause.
items.score_note: Expects the Fed to keep an explicit easing bias; no dates in the quoted passage.
items.call: hold in January; dovish hold with easing bias retained (no dated path in passage)

items.speaker: Barclays economists (FOMC preview; authors not named on page)
items.occasion: Preview of the January 27-28 FOMC, quoted in investingLive bank-by-bank round-up (published Jan 28, 11:48 GMT, before the decision)
items.quote: signal it is in no rush to cut rates further
items.summary: Barclays expected the FOMC to signal it is in no rush to cut again and to describe downside employment risks and upside inflation risks as more balanced; its path was 50bp of cuts in 2026, in June and December.
items.score_note: Two cuts in 2026, the first not before June, with a no-rush message.
items.call: 2026: 50bp, cuts in June and December

items.speaker: BofA economists (FOMC preview; authors not named on page)
items.occasion: Preview of the January 27-28 FOMC, quoted in investingLive bank-by-bank round-up (published Jan 28, 11:48 GMT, before the decision)
items.quote: The Fed is firmly on hold, and the balance of risk hasn't changed.
items.summary: BofA said politics may take center stage at the January meeting, the Fed is firmly on hold with the balance of risk unchanged, and market pricing creates risk of a dovish surprise from Powell; its path was 50bp of cuts in June and July.
items.score_note: Firmly on hold near term but two cuts forecast for mid-2026.
items.call: 2026: 50bp, cuts in June and July

items.speaker: Citi economists (FOMC preview; authors not named on page)
items.occasion: Preview of the January 27-28 FOMC, quoted in investingLive bank-by-bank round-up (published Jan 28, 11:48 GMT, before the decision)
items.quote: the Fed will likely deliver more cuts than are priced
items.summary: Citi said a soft labor market and cooling inflation mean the Fed will likely deliver more cuts over 2026 than the market prices; its path was 75bp, in March, July and September.
items.score_note: Most dovish house in the set: three cuts starting in March, more than priced. March is two meetings away, so between -2 and -1; chose -1.
items.call: 2026: 75bp, cuts in March, July and September

items.speaker: Tiffany Wilding
items.occasion: PIMCO Macro Signposts note after the January FOMC: Fed Holds Steady and Signals Longer-Term Easing Bias
items.quote: We expect the Fed will remain on hold until later this year, when rate cuts are likely to resume.
items.summary: Wilding expects the Fed to stay on hold for now and resume rate cuts later in 2026 as inflation pressures recede with productivity gains, fading tariff effects and softer housing costs.
items.score_note: Cuts expected to resume later in 2026; not imminent.
items.call: on hold until later in 2026, then rate cuts resume

items.speaker: Wells Fargo economists (FOMC preview; authors not named on page)
items.occasion: Preview of the January 27-28 FOMC, quoted in investingLive bank-by-bank round-up (published Jan 28, 11:48 GMT, before the decision)
items.quote: the higher the hurdle becomes to justify on economic grounds the need
items.summary: Wells Fargo kept 50bp of cuts in March and June but said the longer the FOMC waits, the higher the hurdle to justify further easing, and it did not expect Powell to hint at a March cut.
items.score_note: Keeps March and June cuts while conceding the hurdle is rising; chose -1 rather than -2.
items.call: 2026: 50bp, cuts in March and June

items.speaker: J.P. Morgan Wealth Management strategists (not named in quoted passage)
items.occasion: J.P. Morgan Wealth Management web article after the January 28 FOMC
items.quote: Our strategists anticipate one more rate cut this year, in line with consensus.
items.summary: The wealth-management arm (distinct from Feroli's Global Research, which forecasts no cuts) said its strategists do not anticipate a cut until summer and expect one more cut in 2026.
items.score_note: One cut expected in 2026, not before summer. Not the investment-bank research call.
items.call: 2026: one more cut, not before summer

items.speaker: Michael Feroli
items.occasion: J.P. Morgan Global Research web article on the Fed's next move (version dated February 04, 2026, after the January FOMC and Warsh nomination; archived Feb 19)
items.quote: We see the Fed holding the target range for the funds rate steady at 3.5-3.75% for the rest of the year.
items.summary: After the January hold and the Warsh nomination, J.P. Morgan Global Research continued to expect no change in 2026 and a 25bp hike in Q3 2027; Feroli thinks Warsh may not find it easy to persuade the committee to cut.
items.score_note: Unchanged call: hold all year, next move a 2027 hike.
items.call: on hold for the rest of 2026; 25bp hike in Q3 2027

items.speaker: Michael Gapen
items.occasion: Morgan Stanley Thoughts on the Market podcast on the January FOMC (recorded Thursday Feb 5, 8:30am New York)
items.quote: And in our view, it was more of a dovish hold.
items.summary: Gapen read the January meeting as a dovish hold: the Fed still has an easing bias and rates should generally move lower over time, likely when inflation comes down.
items.score_note: Sees an easing bias and lower rates over time; no dated path in the passage.
items.call: dovish hold; Fed keeps an easing bias and cuts later when inflation comes down (no dates in passage)

items.speaker: Stephen Juneau
items.occasion: Reuters poll of economists (published Feb 11)
items.quote: The Fed will cut twice this year under Warsh (but) it's not necessarily due to a clear economic argument,
items.summary: Juneau said BofA expects two cuts in 2026 under Warsh, but not because of a clear economic case; with more expansionary fiscal policy it "could be a recipe for overdoing it".
items.score_note: Forecast is two cuts in 2026 even though he sees weak economic justification.
items.call: 2026: two cuts under Warsh

items.speaker: Citi analysts (note; authors not named on page)
items.occasion: Research note written Tuesday Feb 17 ahead of January FOMC minutes, quoted by Reuters Feb 18
items.quote: The Fed is prepared to lower rates further this year if inflation cools
items.summary: Citi analysts wrote that the Fed is prepared to cut further in 2026 if inflation cools and that this should show up in the January FOMC minutes.
items.score_note: Expects further cuts this year conditional on cooler inflation; no timing on the page.
items.call: further cuts in 2026 if inflation cools (timing not stated on page)

items.speaker: Goldman Sachs economists (note; authors not named on page)
items.occasion: Research note on Wednesday Mar 11, reported by Reuters (copy published Mar 12 HKT)
items.quote: By September, we expect both some further labour market softening and progress on underlying inflation to contribute to the case for a cut,
items.summary: Goldman pushed its two 2026 cuts to September and December from June and September, citing inflation risks from the Middle East conflict; it said earlier cuts remain possible if the labor market weakens sooner, and that oil-driven inflation worries would not stop the Fed easing in that case.
items.score_note: Still two cuts in 2026 but delayed by a quarter; explicitly keeps the door open to earlier cuts. (Page is a Hong Kong reprint of Reuters with British spelling.)
items.call: 2026: two cuts, September and December (previously June and September)

items.speaker: Jeremy Schwartz
items.occasion: Reuters poll of economists (published Mar 12)
items.quote: He can probably get one or two cuts this year.
items.summary: Schwartz said forecasts must factor in what Warsh has told the president he will try to do, but it depends on committee dynamics and data; Warsh can probably get one or two cuts in 2026.
items.score_note: Still expects one or two cuts in 2026 despite war-driven inflation risk.
items.call: 2026: one or two cuts under Warsh

items.speaker: Matthew Luzzetti
items.role: Chief U.S. economist, Deutsche Bank Securities
items.occasion: Research note written the week of Mar 9, quoted by Reuters Mar 16
items.quote: A question that was almost unthinkable two weeks ago is now being more heavily debated: Could the Fed raise rates in 2026?
items.summary: Luzzetti raised the question of a 2026 rate hike after the oil shock; per Reuters he concluded that increases were still unlikely absent a clear jump in inflation expectations.
items.score_note: Raises hike risk but concludes hikes unlikely; between 0 and +1, chose 0.
items.call: 2026 hikes debated but still unlikely absent a clear jump in inflation expectations

items.speaker: Deutsche Bank research (morning note citing its economists; authors not named on page)
items.occasion: Deutsche Bank note ahead of the March 17-18 FOMC, quoted by FXStreet Insights Team (Mar 16, 07:38 GMT)
items.quote: Starting with the Fed, our economists expect them to keep rates unchanged this week and think they’ll emphasise elevated geopolitical uncertainty.
items.summary: Deutsche Bank economists expected a hold in March with emphasis on geopolitical uncertainty and oil-driven inflation risk, and a dot plot still signalling one 2026 cut, though it would not take much to shift the median dot.
items.score_note: Hold call with inflation risk emphasized; no change to the rate path stated. Between 0 and +1, chose 0.
items.call: hold in March; dot plot still expected to show one 2026 cut

items.speaker: BofA economists (FOMC preview; authors not named on page)
items.occasion: Preview of the March 17-18 FOMC, quoted in investingLive bank-by-bank round-up (published Mar 18, 11:15 GMT, before the decision)
items.quote: We don't think the Fed needs to cut any further, but the majority of the committee is still holding on to a low neutral rate
items.summary: BofA said it does not think the Fed needs to cut further, but the committee majority holds a low neutral-rate view, which opens the door to more cuts on any blip in the data, especially with Warsh advocating cuts; its forecast was 25bp cuts in June and July.
items.score_note: Forecast basis: two cuts in June and July, even though BofA itself sees no need for them.
items.call: 2026: 25bp cuts in June and July (hold in March)

items.speaker: Citi economists (FOMC preview; authors not named on page)
items.occasion: Preview of the March 17-18 FOMC, quoted in investingLive bank-by-bank round-up (published Mar 18, 11:15 GMT, before the decision)
items.quote: We see risks tilted dovish at the FOMC meeting.
items.summary: Citi expected Fed officials to treat the oil jump as a temporary supply shock they can look through, with near-zero job growth and slower spending raising concern about employment; it expected an 8-2 hold and 25bp cuts to follow in April, July and September.
items.score_note: Three cuts still forecast, the first at the next meeting after March; most dovish house. Between -2 and -1, chose -1 because the March decision itself was a hold call.
items.call: 2026: 25bp cuts in April, July and September (hold in March)

items.speaker: Goldman Sachs economists (FOMC preview; authors not named on page)
items.occasion: Preview of the March 17-18 FOMC, quoted in investingLive bank-by-bank round-up (published Mar 18, 11:15 GMT, before the decision)
items.quote: For the Fed, the war increases both the risk that earlier rate cuts will be needed to address labour market
items.summary: Goldman expected a 7-3 hold with the statement acknowledging war-related uncertainty, and said the war raises both the risk of earlier cuts to address labor softening and the risk that higher inflation delays cuts; its path was 25bp cuts in September and December.
items.score_note: Two cuts later in 2026 with two-sided risk around timing.
items.call: 2026: 25bp cuts in September and December

items.speaker: J.P. Morgan economists (FOMC preview; authors not named on page)
items.occasion: Preview of the March 17-18 FOMC, quoted in investingLive bank-by-bank round-up (published Mar 18, 11:15 GMT, before the decision)
items.quote: We look for the median dot to continue to look for one cut this year, though
items.summary: J.P. Morgan expected the median dot to keep one 2026 cut, with a little under even odds that it moves to no cut, and said any endorsement of looking through energy inflation would be conditional on stable inflation expectations; its own forecast is no rate change through 2026.
items.score_note: This page states only no change through 2026. The +1 keeps the firm consistent with its own published call (jpmorgan.com versions dated Feb 20 and Apr 17 both give the next move as a Q3 2027 hike); on this page alone it would be 0.
items.call: no rate changes through the whole of 2026

items.speaker: Morgan Stanley strategists (note; authors not named on page)
items.occasion: Research note the morning after the March 18 FOMC, reported by Reuters
items.quote: The primary risk to our view remains that rate cuts come later or not at all,
items.summary: Morgan Stanley pushed its next cut to September from June and now expects quarter-point cuts in September and December 2026, joining Goldman Sachs and Barclays. It flags the risk that cuts come later or not at all, while a second-round oil surge could weaken activity and prompt cuts.
items.score_note: Still two cuts in 2026 but delayed three months, with risk skewed to later/none.
items.call: 2026: two cuts, September and December (previously June and September)

items.speaker: Tiffany Wilding and Graeme Westwood
items.role: Economist, PIMCO (Wilding); co-author Westwood (title not on page)
items.occasion: PIMCO Macro Signposts note after the March FOMC: Caution Takes Center Stage at the March Fed Meeting
items.quote: we still expect to see the Fed remain on hold through most of 2026, before resuming their easing cycle toward a neutral rate just above 3%
items.summary: PIMCO said the Fed signaled continued patience on the timing of cuts; it still expects a hold through most of 2026 before easing resumes toward a neutral rate just above 3%, and sees labor market vulnerabilities as the more material risk.
items.score_note: Easing still expected to resume late in 2026; labor risk emphasized over inflation.
items.call: on hold through most of 2026, then easing resumes toward neutral just above 3%

items.speaker: Lindsay Rosner
items.role: Head of Multi-Sector Investing, Goldman Sachs Asset Management
items.occasion: Goldman Sachs The Markets podcast (recorded March 25, 2026), transcript PDF
items.quote: that they will cut two times this year
items.summary: Rosner (GSAM, the asset-management arm, not GS Research) said the modal case is still two Fed cuts in 2026, out of consensus with a market that had priced a hold, because the Fed looks at core PCE and still weighs the labor market; she does not expect lasting effects that force a hike.
items.score_note: Two cuts in 2026 as the modal case and pushback on hike pricing. Asset-management view.
items.call: 2026: two cuts (modal case); Fed not on hold all year

items.speaker: Jonathan Millar
items.occasion: Reuters poll of economists (published Mar 26)
items.quote: entirely plausible the Fed waits out the oil price for longer and delays cuts into next year.
items.summary: Millar said the Fed will not gain confidence on inflation until September, and that it is plausible cuts get delayed into 2027; he does not think markets (pricing hikes) lead the Fed.
items.score_note: Base case still a first cut in September 2026; flags delay risk and rejects hike pricing.
items.call: first cut September 2026; plausible cuts are delayed into 2027

items.speaker: Michael Gapen
items.occasion: Morgan Stanley Thoughts on the Market podcast on the March FOMC (recorded Thursday Mar 26, 8:30am New York)
items.quote: We've slid those back to September and December.
items.summary: Gapen said the answer to higher macro uncertainty is caution and later cuts: Morgan Stanley moved its cuts from June and September to September and December because higher oil prices mean it takes the Fed longer to conclude disinflation is occurring. He still thinks second-half cuts are reasonable.
items.score_note: Two cuts still forecast for 2026, delayed; same call as the Mar 19 note, restated in public.
items.call: 2026: two cuts, September and December (previously June and September)

items.speaker: Manuel Abecasis
items.role: Analyst, Goldman Sachs (as described on page)
items.occasion: Research note arguing market pricing of 2026 hikes is too high, reported by Investing.com (reprint dated Apr 2)
items.quote: Our probability-weighted Fed forecast remains meaningfully more dovish than market pricing,
items.summary: Abecasis argued the roughly 45% market-implied chance of a 2026 hike overstates the risk: the oil shock is smaller and narrower than past ones, the labor market is softening, the funds rate is already 50-75bp above neutral, and oil shocks have not historically led to Fed tightening.
items.score_note: Pushes back on hike pricing and calls its own forecast more dovish than the market.
items.call: hikes in 2026 unlikely; probability-weighted forecast more dovish than market pricing

items.speaker: Citigroup economists (note; authors not named on page)
items.occasion: Research note dated April 3 after March jobs report, reported by Reuters Apr 6
items.quote: But the timing of upcoming data suggests a later start to rate cuts than we had previously been expecting,
items.summary: Citi pushed back its timeline: 75bp of cuts now in September, October and December 2026 instead of June, July and September, citing persistent inflation risks and strong March job gains; it still expects a weakening labor market to bring cuts later in the year.
items.score_note: Keeps 75bp of 2026 cuts but delays the start by three months.
items.call: 2026: three cuts (75bp), September, October and December (previously June, July and September)

items.speaker: Wells Fargo Investment Institute strategists (not named on page)
items.occasion: Wells Fargo Investment Institute forecast change, reported by Reuters
items.quote: we believe that the balance of risks has shifted to incentivize patience from the Fed,
items.summary: Wells Fargo Investment Institute (the wealth-side strategy arm, not Wells Fargo Economics) dropped its forecast of two 2026 cuts and now expects none, citing a noticeable but likely transient inflation bump and geopolitical uncertainty.
items.score_note: Moves to no cuts in 2026 (hold); no hike call.
items.call: no cuts in 2026 (previously two cuts)

items.speaker: Wells Fargo economists (not named on page)
items.occasion: Wells Fargo research note quoted by FXStreet Insights Team (Apr 8)
items.quote: we have pushed out the start of easing but still expect 50 bps of total cuts this year
items.summary: Wells Fargo economists pushed back the start of easing because of higher oil prices and stickier inflation, but still expect 50bp of cuts in 2026, now at the September and December meetings; they see the next move as more likely a cut than a hike, with risks skewed to later and/or less easing.
items.score_note: Keeps two cuts in 2026, delayed to September and December; says a cut is more likely than a hike. Differs from Wells Fargo Investment Institute, which dropped 2026 cuts on Apr 6.
items.call: 2026: 50bp, 25bp cuts in September and December (start of easing pushed out)

items.speaker: UBS Global Wealth Management analysts (not named on page)
items.occasion: UBS GWM comment ahead of March CPI, quoted in Reuters stock-market report (Apr 10)
items.quote: we continue to believe that the central bank remains on track to cut rates later this year,
items.summary: UBS Global Wealth Management said that although Fed officials expect higher oil prices to delay disinflation, it still believes the Fed is on track to cut later in 2026, expecting sequential core inflation to cool as tariff effects fade and labor demand falls.
items.score_note: Maintains cuts later in 2026 after the oil shock; a month later it pushed the first cut to December.
items.call: Fed on track to cut later in 2026 (timing not stated on page)

items.speaker: Michael Gapen
items.occasion: Morgan Stanley Thoughts on the Market podcast, economics roundtable part 1 (recorded Tuesday Apr 14, 10am New York)
items.quote: That should open the door for the Fed to cut two times this year.
items.summary: Gapen said oil shocks have limited second-round effects on core inflation, tariff pass-through will moderate and core inflation should ease later in the year, opening the door to two cuts in 2026; he said raising rates would be the wrong thing to do.
items.score_note: Baseline two cuts later in 2026 and explicit opposition to hiking; two weeks before the firm dropped the cuts.
items.call: 2026: two cuts later this year

items.speaker: Michael Feroli
items.occasion: J.P. Morgan Global Research web article on the Fed's next move (version dated April 17, 2026; archived Apr 30)
items.quote: It should make the late April FOMC meeting an easy call for the Committee to stay on hold.
items.summary: J.P. Morgan Global Research expects a hold on April 28-29 and for the rest of 2026, then a 25bp hike in Q3 2027; it says the Fed could cut if the labor market weakens significantly or the energy fallout becomes more severe. Feroli calls the Fed's patience a key cushion for financial conditions.
items.score_note: Unchanged call through the oil shock: hold in 2026, next move a 2027 hike; cut risk acknowledged.
items.call: hold on April 28-29 and for the rest of 2026; 25bp hike in Q3 2027

items.speaker: Brett Ryan
items.occasion: Reuters poll of economists (published Apr 22), after Warsh confirmation hearing
items.quote: they really need to be careful of inflation expectations
items.summary: Ryan said Warsh is one voice and would need time to earn the committee's trust before cutting quickly, and that after five years of missing the target the Fed must guard against unanchored inflation expectations.
items.score_note: No dated rate path on the page; stresses inflation-expectations risk and no quick cuts. Between 0 and +1, chose 0.
items.call: no quick cuts under Warsh (no dated path on page)

items.speaker: Michael Gapen
items.occasion: Reuters poll of economists (Apr 2026, published Apr 22)
items.quote: tariff inflation is transitory and oil puts upward pressure on headline inflation but doesn't translate into faster core inflation
items.summary: Gapen said tariff inflation is transitory and oil lifts headline but not core inflation, so the Fed can ease later in 2026; the main risk is inflation does not behave and the Fed just stays on hold.
items.score_note: Still forecasts easing later in 2026 one week before dropping the call.
items.call: Fed eases later in 2026; risk is the Fed just stays on hold

items.speaker: Kay Haigh
items.role: Global co-head of fixed income and liquidity solutions, Goldman Sachs Asset Management
items.occasion: Emailed comment after the April 29 FOMC decision (Reuters instant view)
items.quote: This balance could see rates being brought back down to neutral later this year
items.summary: Haigh (GSAM, the asset-management arm, not GS Research) said the Fed is in a stable place, upside inflation risks have increased, and rates could still be brought back to neutral later in 2026 unless Iran re-escalates and energy prices rise.
items.score_note: Still sees room for cuts later in 2026, conditional; asset-management view, not the GS Research house call.
items.call: rates could be brought down to neutral later in 2026; restrictive for longer if Iran re-escalates

items.speaker: Morgan Stanley economists (note; authors not named on page)
items.occasion: Research note on Wednesday Apr 29 after the April FOMC, reported by Reuters Apr 30
items.quote: to continued strength in growth and labor markets, reducing the urgency for further policy easing
items.summary: Morgan Stanley dropped its forecast of two quarter-point cuts in 2026 and now expects no cuts this year, saying inflation above target and continued strength in growth and labor markets reduce the urgency for further easing.
items.score_note: Moves from two 2026 cuts to none; a hold forecast, not a hike call.
items.call: no cuts in 2026 (previously two quarter-point cuts)

items.speaker: Tiffany Wilding
items.occasion: PIMCO Macro Signposts note after the April FOMC: Holding Pattern Continues Amid Competing Risks
items.quote: Our view remains that the next move will be a rate cut, but the timing is far from clear.
items.summary: Wilding read the three dissents against the easing bias as a hawkish lean but still expects the next move to be a cut, sees a high bar for hikes, and says a more persistent energy shock would delay cuts.
items.score_note: Next move still a cut but with no timing and no longer tied to 2026; high bar for hikes. Between -1 and 0, chose 0.
items.call: next move a cut, timing unclear; high bar for a hike

items.speaker: Barclays economists (note; authors not named on page)
items.occasion: Research note after the April 29 FOMC, quoted in Reuters round-up Apr 30
items.quote: skewed toward delayed rate cuts
items.summary: Barclays kept a baseline of one 25bp cut in September 2026 but said risks are skewed toward delayed rate cuts.
items.score_note: Baseline still one cut in 2026, with risk of delay; four days later it dropped the cut.
items.call: 2026: one 25bp cut in September; risks skewed toward delayed cuts

items.speaker: Citi analysts (note; authors not named on page)
items.occasion: Research note after the April 29 FOMC, quoted by Reuters Apr 30
items.quote: cuts can be rapidly priced back in by markets if oil prices fall.
items.summary: Citi continued to project that cooler inflation and renewed loosening in labor markets will lead to rate reductions starting in September, and said cuts can be quickly priced back in if oil falls.
items.score_note: Keeps cuts from September 2026 after the hawkish April meeting.
items.call: cuts beginning September 2026 (maintained)

items.speaker: Barclays analysts (note; authors not named on page)
items.occasion: Research note Monday May 4, reported by Reuters
items.quote: We expect the higher and more prolonged oil price trajectory to boost both headline and core PCE inflation measures
items.summary: Barclays dropped its September 2026 cut and now expects no easing in 2026, keeping one quarter-point cut in March 2027. It said a sudden rise in unemployment would bring faster and more aggressive cuts.
items.score_note: Moves to no cuts in 2026 (hold); next move still a cut in March 2027.
items.call: no cuts in 2026 (previously one cut in September 2026); one 25bp cut in March 2027

items.speaker: BofA analysts (note; authors not named on page)
items.occasion: Research note dated May 8 after April jobs report, reported by Reuters May 11
items.quote: We think (incoming Fed Chair) Warsh will push for lower rates, but the data flow precludes cuts
items.summary: BofA now expects the Fed on hold for the rest of 2026, with two 25bp cuts in July and September 2027; it said Warsh will push for lower rates but the data preclude cuts for now, and cuts should be in play by next summer.
items.score_note: Moves to no cuts in 2026 (hold); next move still a cut in 2027.
items.call: on hold for the rest of 2026; two 25bp cuts in July and September 2027

items.speaker: Goldman Sachs analysts (note; authors not named on page)
items.occasion: Research note dated May 8 after April jobs report, reported by Reuters May 11
items.quote: if the labor market does not weaken sufficiently this year, we would instead expect the FOMC to deliver two final cuts in 2027,
items.summary: Goldman pushed its cuts to December 2026 and March 2027 from a first cut in September 2026, and said that if the labor market does not weaken enough this year the two final cuts would both come in 2027.
items.score_note: Baseline still has one cut in December 2026, but delayed and conditional on labor weakening; between -1 and 0, kept -1 because a 2026 cut remains the base case.
items.call: cuts in December 2026 and March 2027 (previously first cut September 2026)

items.speaker: Andrew Dubinsky (lead author) and UBS GWM analysts
items.role: Analyst, UBS Global Wealth Management (as described on page)
items.occasion: UBS GWM note on Tuesday May 12, reported by Reuters May 13
items.quote: The conditions needed to justify a September move—particularly sustained core goods disinflation and reduced supply-side uncertainty—have not yet been met,
items.summary: UBS Global Wealth Management pushed its 25bp cuts to December 2026 and March 2027 from September and December 2026, saying conditions for a September move are not met and growth and labor conditions reduce urgency.
items.score_note: Still one cut in December 2026 in the base case, delayed by a quarter.
items.call: cuts in December 2026 and March 2027 (previously September and December 2026)

items.speaker: Seth Carpenter
items.role: Global Chief Economist and Head of Macro Research, Morgan Stanley
items.occasion: Morgan Stanley Thoughts on the Market podcast, mid-year global economic outlook (recorded Thursday May 14, 10am New York)
items.quote: We expect the Fed to now stay on hold all the way through 2026
items.summary: Carpenter said central banks have become less accommodative as inflation risks rose; Morgan Stanley expects the Fed on hold through 2026 and, if inflation does come down, two cuts in the first half of 2027.
items.score_note: Hold through 2026; next move still a cut in 2027.
items.call: on hold through 2026; two cuts in the first half of 2027 if inflation comes down

items.speaker: Aditya Bhave
items.role: Head of U.S. economics, Bank of America
items.occasion: Reuters poll of economists (May 14-19)
items.quote: It feels like if they are going to have their next move as a cut, it's more likely to be next year than this year,
items.summary: Bhave said both hikes and cuts are feasible, the base case is a hold and it is a close call between the other two; if the next move is a cut it is more likely in 2027 than 2026.
items.score_note: Base case hold with two-sided risk; explicitly says hikes are feasible but not the base case.
items.call: base case hold; hikes and cuts both feasible; a cut more likely in 2027 than 2026

items.speaker: Phillip Lee
items.role: Head of Real Money Rate Sales, Goldman Sachs Global Banking & Markets
items.occasion: Goldman Sachs The Markets podcast (recorded May 21, 2026), transcript PDF
items.quote: the Fed will stay on hold for a bit
items.summary: Lee (a sales-desk view, not GS Research) said the base case has moved from when and how much the Fed cuts to how long it stays on hold; he finds the roughly 30bp of hikes priced into 2027 a bit tough, though inflation keeps the Fed on hold at best.
items.score_note: Base case is a hold of uncertain length; notes hikes are priced but does not forecast them.
items.firm: Goldman Sachs Global Banking & Markets (rates sales)
items.call: on hold for a while; base case shifted from cuts to how long the hold lasts

items.speaker: Nomura economists (note; authors not named on page)
items.occasion: Research note dated May 21, reported by Invezz May 22
items.quote: But recent data and Fedspeak make us sceptical that he will be able to convince a majority of the FOMC to go along with rate cuts in 2026.
items.summary: Nomura dropped its forecast of two cuts later in 2026 and now expects no cuts this year, citing higher inflation readings and waning support among Fed officials for easing; it doubts Warsh can win an FOMC majority for cuts.
items.score_note: Moves to no cuts in 2026 (hold); no hike call on the page.
items.call: no cuts in 2026 (previously two cuts later in the year)

coverage_notes: Sources actually opened: Reuters copies on Kitco (off-the-wire sitemap scanned for all of Jan-May 2026) and BNN Bloomberg (daily sitemaps Jan-May), The Standard HK, The Star, Invezz, Hellenic Shipping News (Investing.com reprints), FXStreet (Wells Fargo research), investingLive (weekly sitemaps W01-W23; its bank-by-bank FOMC previews of Jan 28 and Mar 18 carry direct quotations, none found for Apr 29), and firm pages: jpmorgan.com Global Research Fed page via four Wayback versions, morganstanley.com Thoughts on the Market transcripts, pimco.com post-FOMC notes, goldmansachs.com insights and transcript PDFs. Timeline of the turn as supported by the items: J.P. Morgan had no 2026 cuts from Jan 9 (next move a Q3 2027 hike) and did not change through May. Goldman: Mar/Jun -> Jun/Sep (Jan 11) -> Sep/Dec (Mar 11) -> Dec 2026/Mar 2027 (May 8); it dropped 2026 cuts only on Jun 9, outside the window. Morgan Stanley: Jan/Apr -> Jun/Sep (Jan 9) -> Sep/Dec (Mar 19) -> no 2026 cuts (Apr 29). Barclays: Mar/Jun -> Jun/Dec (Jan 12) -> Sep only (Mar 13) -> no 2026 cuts (May 4). BofA: Jun/Jul (Jan through Mar 18) -> first cut September (date not found) -> no 2026 cuts, Jul/Sep 2027 (May 8). Citi: Mar/Jul/Sep (Jan-Feb) -> Apr/Jul/Sep (Mar 18) -> Jun/Jul/Sep (date not found) -> Sep/Oct/Dec (Apr 3), still cutting in 2026 at end-May. Wells Fargo Economics: Mar/Jun (Jan 14) -> Sep/Dec (by Apr 8); Wells Fargo Investment Institute separately went to no cuts (Apr 6). Nomura: Jun/Sep -> Sep/Dec (Apr 8, paraphrase only) -> no 2026 cuts (May 21). UBS GWM: cuts later in 2026 (Apr 10; Sep/Dec per Reuters) -> Dec 2026/Mar 2027 (May 12). No house in this set had a 2026 HIKE as its base case inside the window; the most hawkish were J.P. Morgan (2027 hike) and commentary that hikes were 'feasible' (BofA, May 19) or debated (Deutsche, mid-March). Scoring convention used for forecasts: base case with a 2026 cut that is not at the next meeting = -1; hold through 2026 with next move a cut = 0; next move a hike but distant = +1; an explicit call for cuts now = -2 (only Rieder, scored as 'should'). Dates: where the page gives the note date it is used (date_basis event); otherwise the article date. Several Reuters poll quotes carry the poll publication date. Quotes from Kitco pages are deliberately cut to spans that contain no zero-width characters (Reuters copies embed U+200B/U+2060 inside sentences), so some quotes are clauses rather than full sentences. The Goldman Mar 11 quote is from a Hong Kong reprint that uses British spelling ('labour'); the Nomura May 21 quote likewise ('sceptical'). Two Goldman-arm items come from transcript PDFs, and the investingLive preview pages wrap quotations across lines, so those quotes are kept to a single text line. Thin coverage: Deutsche Bank (3 items, no dated change of its one-cut-in-September call found), Nomura (3), UBS (2, wealth management only; no UBS Global Research item), BlackRock (1 Rieder item; his March 25 Bloomberg remarks are paywalled), and February in general (no forecast changes; the Feb 6 factbox shows calls unchanged after the January FOMC). No CNBC or Bloomberg TV transcript was opened. Items labelled Goldman Sachs Asset Management, Goldman Sachs Global Banking & Markets (rates sales), J.P. Morgan Wealth Management and Wells Fargo Investment Institute are other arms of those firms, not the research house call; filter on firm if only the sell-side economists are wanted. Roles verified on opened pages: Michael Feroli chief U.S. economist (J.P. Morgan), Michael Gapen chief U.S. economist and Seth Carpenter global chief economist (Morgan Stanley), David Mericle chief US economist (Goldman Sachs; Jan Hatzius is named as team lead by Bloomberg), Aditya Bhave head of U.S. economics (BofA), Matthew Luzzetti chief U.S. economist (Deutsche Bank Securities), Jonathan Millar senior U.S. economist (Barclays; Stocktwits names Marc Giannoni as chief U.S. economist), Jeremy Schwartz senior U.S. economist (Nomura), Tiffany Wilding economist (PIMCO), Rick Rieder head of global fixed income (BlackRock). Not verified from any opened page: chief economists of Citi (Reuters copy via Bloomberg names Andrew Hollenhorst as a Citigroup economist), UBS, Wells Fargo.
